<<The Evening That Changed Everything>>

The stadium lights of Bishworth had long since faded from Morgan Rogers' mind, yet the echo of his own breathing still lingered in the quiet of the dressing room. He sat on the edge of his familiar bench, laces undone, staring at a pair of worn boots as if they belonged to someone else.

A week ago, he'd been another promising forward in a crowd of talented players. Now, his name had become a phrase repeated on every football radio show in the country. "Jonah Lomu in his prime." "Robustness." "Running power." The words swirled around him like leaves in an autumn wind, and he felt simultaneously elated and unsettled.

His phone buzzed on the bench. A message from his mum: *"Saw you on the news, sweetheart. You looked brilliant out there. Proud of you."* Another followed from his best friend since primary school: *"Bro you were MIGHTY against them. Partey looked like he was 80. Love you."*

Morgan exhaled slowly. The initial wave of disappointment — that sour, bitter taste he felt stepping off the pitch, as though the game hadn't gone exactly to plan — had given way to something warmer. His teammates had been on top of him, slapping his back, pointing at the pitch and laughing about the Partey incident. The media had flooded in after the match, cameras flashing, microphones thrust toward a young man who found himself the centre of a conversation he'd never expected to be part of.

He'd gone home and replayed the clips. The tackle on Declan Rice. The moment he'd beckoned Partey forward, only to slide his foot through and send him stumbling. The shot that had kissed the post by a matter of inches. Each replay added a layer of understanding to that strange feeling he'd carried in the car back to Stoke: the "weird spot."

Not the spot of a star. The spot of a man who'd finally believed the words in his own head.

*"Why not me?"*

It was a simple thought. But over the following months, it had become an anchor, something he returned to when the league table was brutal, when the press was unkind, when a world-class midfielder on the opposing team seemed to make every pass look effortless. *Why not me?* The question wasn't arrogance. It was permission. Permission to be the one who ran an extra ten metres. Permission to win the second ball. Permission to believe that on a given Tuesday in November, the best player on the pitch could very well be the one wearing the red number 11.

Morgan pulled his phone from his pocket and set it face-down. There was a training session in four days, and a lot of work to do. But as he laced up his boots again, there was a telling smile forming on his face — the same smile Mikel Arteta had seen in the tunnel that evening.

The showreel, he knew, was only in its infancy.

<<Partey's Tuesday>>

Thomas Partey had been a professional footballer for over a decade. He had played at Barcelona's La Masia. He had walked onto pitch at the World Cup final in Qatar. He had faced defenders on the other end of the field who were a full size bigger, twice as fast, or simply a different species of athletic creature.

But on a Tuesday evening at Villa Park, something had happened that he could not yet explain.

A young forward with the build of a sprinter and the confidence of a man who had decided, somewhere between the second half and the post-match interview, that he could be the best player on the pitch. A young forward who had, with a casual flick of his wrist, put a former Barcelona academy product on all fours and sent a clip of that moment circulating at 200,000 views in an afternoon.

Partey sat in his hotel room in Birmingham, ice on his knee, a towel draped over his head. His phone was in his hand. Declan Rice was on the screen, watching the same clip. They had been in the same squad for years. They had been in the same dressing room when Mikel had been appointed. And now they were both on a highlight reel of a young man wringing them out.

"You look like an old man," Declan had said, barely a laugh in it.

"You look like you're about to retire," Partey had replied.

They both looked at the next clip. Gabriel Martinelli trying to get past Rogers, who simply... brushed him off. Not a big movement. Not a hero's tackle. Just a shoulder, a step, a small and almost indifferent gesture that sent a two-time European Championship winner stumbling.

Partey set his phone down. The ice was melting. The towel was no longer necessary.

He thought about the conversation he'd have with Mikel the next morning. Not a critique, exactly. A conversation about what had changed in that final thirty minutes of the first half. How the game had shifted, how the young man had read the space, how Partey had seen him coming and still been put away.

He thought about the "Jonah Lomu" comparison. It was a generous thing to say. Lomu had been a different sport, a different era, a different body. But the essence of it was there: that moment where the young man had simply been *more*, in every physical sense, and the rest of them had had to adjust.

Partey was not a bitter man. He was not a sore loser. He had faced much larger opponents, in much louder contexts, and he had come away with a trophy and a few silver medals and a long career behind him. He was not upset.

He was, however, curious.

In three days, Arsenal would travel to a different ground, face a different team. Partey would run again. He would make his runs. He would put in his hours at the gym. But there was a new variable in the equation now, a young man whose name was being spoken in the context of "what's coming next" and whose quiet, almost shy smile in the post-match interview suggested he already knew.

Partey stood up, grabbed a glass of water, and walked to the window. The city lights of Birmingham were a soft blur against the November dark. Somewhere out there, in a house in Stoke, a young man was probably replaying that clip of the post miss for the eleventh time. Thinking about what he could have done differently. Thinking about the "Why not me?" that would be the quiet engine of the next season.

Partey took a sip of water. He was not threatened. He was simply aware. And tomorrow morning, at 8:15 in the training ground, he would run a little faster. He would make a pass a fraction sharper. He would meet that young man in the middle of the pitch and give him everything.

Because that was the game. That was always the game.

And the showreel, for both of them, was still in its infancy.
